source: "The ROI of AI-assisted Software Development" (report version v. 2026.1, 60 pages). Publisher: DORA (Google Cloud), a joint effort with Google Cloud's delta consulting practice. Authors listed: Eva Dong, Andre Ellis Jr., Nathen Harvey, Vivian Hu, Ursula Löbbert-Passing, Eric Maxwell, Aaron Wanjala. Date: PDF created 22 April 2026; landing page says "Last updated: April 22, 2026"; report says "Unless otherwise noted, all citations retrieved February, 2026." URLs opened: https://dora.dev/ai/roi/report (landing page) and https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/dora-roi-of-ai-assisted-software-development-2026.pdf (full PDF). The PDF states the licence as CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
data_type: Model. A financial framework plus a sample ROI calculator with assumed inputs. No new data collection; it borrows the direction of effects from the DORA 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development survey and cites market studies (several from Google Cloud).
sample_and_method: No sample of its own. The method is a one-year ROI model: ROI (%) = (Value - Investment) / Investment. Value = headcount reinvestment capacity + revenue from extra feature deployments + revenue or costs avoided by reducing downtime. Investment = direct hard costs (licences, extra AI/token costs, training, infrastructure) + a J-Curve cost (staff size x salary x productivity drop x duration/12). The worked example uses a hypothetical organisation: 500 technical FTE, $176,000 fully loaded salary, $100M portfolio revenue, $100k cost of downtime per hour, 50 deployments and 50 features a year rising to 56 (a 12% increase), 33% idea success rate, 0.5% revenue impact per successful feature, change failure rate rising from 5% to 6%, 4-hour failed deployment recovery time, 12.5% net time saved per developer, $250 licence + $80 extra AI costs + $9,600 training per user, $100,000 infrastructure, a 15% J-Curve drop lasting three months. Effect directions come from the DORA 2025 survey (4,867 respondents, fieldwork June 13 to July 21, 2025, per that report). The report calls its own numbers "a high-uncertainty estimate meant to spark a conversation, rather than a rigid mathematical formula."
vendor_interest: Yes. Google Cloud sells AI models, AI tooling and cloud infrastructure, and the report advertises Google Cloud Consulting's delta team ("Reach out to us to go beyond the calculator") and cites Google Cloud customer ROI figures. DORA is a Google Cloud programme.
headline_figures: All from the PDF as printed. (1) Sample result: "These estimates in the calculator yield a 39% ROI." (First year investment $8.4M, first year return $11.6M, first year benefit $3.3M; appendix gives $3,281,000 benefit, $8,365,000 investment, $11,646,000 total first year value.) (2) Payback: "In our sample ROI calculator, this gives us a payback period of 0.7 years, which is eight months." (3) Value breakdown: "In our example, if we assume a fully loaded salary of $176k ... that gives us $11M of savings" (headcount reinvestment capacity); revenue from extra features "would give almost $1M of additional revenue" (appendix: $990,000); the downtime calculation "gives us an additional cost (negative value) of $344k—because we assumed the CFR would go up." (4) Costs: "These estimates yield $5,065,000 as the calculated value for the total hard costs (tooling and training)." and "These estimates yield $3,300,000 as the calculated value for the J-Curve cost." (5) J-Curve assumption: "J-Curve productivity drop: 15%" and "J-Curve productivity drop timeline: Three months". (6) Time saved: "the estimates vary between 40 minutes and 150 minutes per day in software development. The sample calculator uses a conservative estimate of 12.5% or about one hour of an eight-hour working day." (7) Instability assumption: "The sample calculator uses 6%, a 20% increase over the baseline of 5%." (8) Restated from DORA 2025 (verified in that report): "the 2025 DORA report, which found that more than 80% of survey respondents reported a perception that AI had increased their productivity." (9) Market figures restated from other sources, not verified against their primaries [uncertain]: "78% of executives report realizing a return on investment from at least one gen AI use case. Furthermore, 88% of early adopters utilizing agentic AI are already seeing positive returns" (Google Cloud, ROI of AI 2025); "while artificial intelligence yields a 35–40% productivity gain on simple, greenfield tasks, its impact on complex, legacy brownfield code is often 10% or less" (cited to Stanford Software Engineering Productivity Research); "Google Cloud customers found an average of 727% return on their investment in Google Cloud AI in three years"; inference costs "dropping by a factor of 280 between November 2022 and October 2024" (Stanford AI Index); "the average payback period for businesses adopting artificial intelligence tools is about eight months" (Google Cloud). (10) Turnover: "replacing a developer can cost 1.5 to 2 times their annual salary" (no citation given; excluded from the calculator). I re-ran the arithmetic: 500 x $176,000 x 12.5% = $11.0M; (50 x 5% x 4 x $100k) - (56 x 6% x 4 x $100k) = -$344k; ($250 + $80 + $9,600) x 500 + $100,000 = $5,065,000; 500 x $176,000 x 15% x 3/12 = $3.3M; $3,281,000 / $8,365,000 = 39%. All match.
metric_layer: Covers every layer and is explicit about the chain between them. Input/usage: AI adoption, licence and token costs. Capabilities: the seven DORA AI Capabilities (the report says "AI adoption needs to be underpinned by capabilities in order to improve DORA key metrics"). Delivery: throughput (lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time) and instability (change failure rate, rework). Non-financial value: productivity, developer experience, user experience, which it calls leading indicators. Financial outcome: cost savings (framed as cost avoided, i.e. not hiring) and revenue, which it calls lagging indicators. It also proposes experiment frequency and deployment frequency as leading metrics and change failure rate and rework as a "stability gauge".
respondent_role_split: None. The report has no respondents of its own and gives no figures by IC, manager, director or executive. The calculator's staff count covers "all roles that may use AI", including product managers, engineers, designers, tech leads and SREs.
workload_signal: Strong qualitative signal, no measured hours. The "verification tax": "Developers invest time reviewing generated code due to concerns about the trustworthiness of output and hallucinations. Furthermore, the tools increase the sheer volume of code produced, which expands the overall review burden." Restating DORA 2025: "burnout remains stubbornly resistant to purely technological solutions" and "AI does not necessarily make friction vanish; rather, the friction moves." The J-Curve dip is modelled as an assumed 15% capacity loss for three months. On headcount: "We strongly recommend organizations do not adopt a headcount-reduction strategy, which has a negative impact on morale and organizational culture, can reduce efficiencies, and can even incentivize workers to not improve their work processes." No figures on pressure to use AI.
definition_of_value_offered: Yes, in detail. Paying off means first-year ROI and payback period computed from a value model that runs left to right: AI adoption, underpinned by capabilities, improves DORA delivery metrics; those show up first as non-financial value (productivity, developer experience, user experience) and later as revenue or cost. Value = headcount reinvestment capacity (staff x salary x net time saved, explicitly cost avoided, not payroll cut) + revenue from extra successful features + revenue or costs avoided through less downtime, which can be negative (the "instability tax"). Investment includes a J-Curve "tuition cost" as well as licences, tokens, training and infrastructure. It warns against double counting the same saved hour and admits the levers differ in "solidity": "Tying an increase in deployments to a revenue lift is speculative and may be challenged by a CFO." It recommends scenario multipliers (conservative 0.8 value / 1.5 cost; optimistic 1.2 value / 0.8 cost). Framing line: "We don't measure AI by the code it writes but by the bottlenecks it clears." Its five-pillar value framework (cost efficiency, productivity, developer experience, user experience, business growth) is adapted from Google Cloud's FinOps value framework.
removal_counterfactual: None. The report offers no evidence on what happens when tools are withdrawn. It stresses the need for a pre-adoption baseline instead: "it is difficult to measure the direct impact of AI without an understanding of 'before.' Do you have a baseline?"
key_quotes: 1) "We don't measure AI by the code it writes but by the bottlenecks it clears." 2) "Think of this dip as the tuition cost of transformation."
caveats: (a) It is a model with assumed inputs, not a measurement; the report says the J-Curve's depth and duration "remain unpredictable". (b) My own reading of the worked example: $11.0M of the $11.646M value (about 94%) is headcount reinvestment capacity, a notional figure driven almost entirely by the assumed 12.5% net time saved. It is capacity, not cash. With the sample inputs the instability term is negative (-$344k), so delivery changes subtract value; the 39% ROI rests on the time-saved assumption. (c) The payback formula as printed (first year investment / first year return) is a ratio, not a time-to-recover calculation; it yields 0.7 only because the return is annual. (d) The claim that AI's instability effect was "second largest" and that "developers spend less time on greater software instability than they gained on individual effectiveness" is an inference from standardised survey coefficients in DORA 2025, which that report itself calls comparisons rather than causal effects. (e) Supporting market figures (78%, 88%, 727%, eight-month payback) come from Google Cloud's own studies, and the 35-40% vs 10% greenfield/brownfield figure and the 280x inference cost drop are second-hand; none were opened [uncertain]. (f) The turnover cost (1.5 to 2 times salary) has no citation. (g) Licence mismatch: the PDF says CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, the dora.dev site footer says CC BY 4.0.
access: Primary opened in full: the 60-page PDF (v. 2026.1) was downloaded and read end to end as extracted text, and the landing page was opened. Not opened: the interactive calculator at dora.dev/ai/roi/calculator, the errata page, and every secondary source the report cites (Google Cloud ROI of AI 2025, MIT NANDA, Stanford AI Index, Stanford SE productivity research, Google Cloud 727% study, Howdy.com salary figure). Figure 5 (the value model diagram) is an image; its content is known only from the surrounding text.
